name: INA821IDR
title: INA821: precision instrumentation amplifier, 35 µV offset, 7 nV/√Hz, 4.7 MHz, one resistor sets the gain
summary: A three-op-amp style instrumentation amplifier with a current-feedback bipolar (super-beta) input stage and a difference-amplifier output stage. One resistor between the two RG pins sets the gain from 1 to 10000 (G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG); with no resistor the gain is 1. Input stage offset is 35 µV max with 0.4 µV/°C drift, input noise 7 nV/√Hz, bias current 0.5 nA max, and the inputs survive ±40 V. It runs from 4.5 V to 36 V (±2.25 V to ±18 V) on 650 µA max and is specified from -40 °C to +125 °C in 8-pin SOIC, VSSOP and WSON.

circuits.title: Example application, G = 10 V/V, 1 V output
circuits.description: A differential source of VDIFF = VOUT / G rides on a 10 V common-mode voltage and reaches the inputs through source resistances of 1 kΩ and 0.99 kΩ. 5.49 kΩ across the RG pins sets G = 10, so the output is 1 V for 100 mV in. The amplifier runs on ±15 V with C1 and C2 bypassing the supply pins to ground; REF is grounded.

parts.note: upper cell of the differential source; VD1 and VD2 in series give VDIFF = VOUT / G
lower cell of the differential source

circuits.title: Op amp buffering a divider for the reference pin
circuits.description: On a single 5 V supply the reference is set at mid-supply by two 100 kΩ resistors, filtered by 1 µF, and buffered by an OPA191 wired as a follower, so REF sees a low-impedance source instead of the divider. RG sets the gain; -VS is grounded.

circuits.title: Bias current return for a floating coil source
circuits.description: A floating source such as a microphone or hydrophone connects across the two inputs, and each input returns to ground through its own 47 kΩ resistor, giving the bias currents a path and keeping the input balanced. RG sets the gain and REF is grounded.

parts.note: sets the gain: G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG

circuits.title: Bias current return for a thermocouple
circuits.description: A thermocouple has a low source resistance, so one 10 kΩ resistor from the non-inverting input to ground is enough to return both bias currents. RG sets the gain and REF is grounded.

parts.note: sets the gain: G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG

circuits.title: Bias current return through a centre-tapped transformer
circuits.description: A transformer couples the signal in; the ends of its secondary go to the two inputs and the secondary's centre tap is grounded, which returns the bias currents. RG sets the gain and REF is grounded.

parts.note: primary P1, P2; secondary S1, S2; centre tap CT
sets the gain: G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG

circuits.title: PLC input, ±10 V or 4 mA to 20 mA (±20 mA)
circuits.description: A three-terminal PLC input. A voltage on the ±10 V terminal is divided by R1 (100 kΩ) and R2 (4.17 kΩ); a current on the ±20 mA terminal flows through R3 (20 Ω) to the ground terminal. Either way the amplifier sees at most ±400 mV between -IN and +IN (+IN sits on the ground terminal). RG = 10.4 kΩ gives G = 5.75, and a REF5025 holds REF at 2.5 V, so the output spans 2.5 V ±2.3 V (0.2 V to 4.8 V). The amplifier runs on ±15 V; the reference runs from 15 V with 1 µF on its output, noise-reduction pin and input.

parts.note: 10.5 kΩ, a standard 0.1 % value, is used

circuits.title: 3-wire RTD interface with analog linearization
circuits.description: A Pt100 RTD and a fixed 100 Ω arm (100 Ω in parallel with 100 kΩ) are each fed from the REF5050's 5 V through a 4.99 kΩ resistor; the RTD node drives +IN and the fixed arm drives -IN. The third RTD lead and REF return to ground. 801 Ω across RG sets the gain. 105 kΩ in series with 1.18 kΩ feeds the output back to the RTD node to linearize the response. The output reads 0 V at 0 °C and 5 V at 200 °C (25 mV/°C), with standard 1 % values in series and parallel and under 0.02 °C error over the span. The amplifier runs on ±15 V; the REF5050 runs from 15 V with 1 µF on its output, NR pin and input.

parts.value: VOUT, 0 V at 0 °C, 5 V at 200 °C, 25 mV/°C

operation.text: A current-feedback input stage feeds a four-resistor difference amplifier. Super-beta NPN transistors Q1 and Q2 buffer the inputs and impose the differential input voltage across RG; the resulting current runs through RG and the two 25 kΩ resistors R1 and R2 in the feedback of A1 and A2. A3, with 40 kΩ resistors, removes the common-mode part and refers the output to REF. Because of VBE and the drop across R1 and R2, the outputs of A1 and A2 sit about 0.8 V below the input voltages. The input RFI filter has a -3 dB frequency of 45 MHz.

Each input has two series FETs that look like a low resistance in normal use, so noise is unaffected, and that limit the current to about 8 mA when the input is overdriven. Each input withstands ±40 V on its own: -40 V on one and +40 V on the other does no harm. In overload the current leaves through the protection diodes to the rails; if the supplies cannot absorb it, zener clamps from each rail to ground (ZD1, ZD2) give it a path to ground.

The internal resistors' tolerance and temperature coefficient are inside the gain error and gain drift figures; RG's own tolerance and drift add to them through the gain equation. The best drift, 5 ppm/°C max, is at G = 1 with no RG, where only the mismatch of the 10 kΩ resistors in A3 matters. Above G = 1 the 24.7 kΩ feedback resistors drift against RG. At gains of about 100 and above, RG is small enough that wiring and socket resistance add gain error, possibly unstable. Parasitic capacitance above a few picofarads on the RG pins threatens stability, and parasitics on the two RG pins need to match to keep CMRR over frequency.

EMIRR is given from 10 MHz to 6 GHz for differential and common-mode interference. Extra EMI filtering near the system inputs may still be needed, with short traces, low-pass filters, damping resistors and parallel, shielded signal routing.

The linear input range reaches to within 2 V of either supply, and CMRR holds across it. At G = 1, CMRR stays above 92 dB anywhere in the common-mode range. The usable range also depends on the differential input, the gain and VREF; The curves of input common-mode voltage against output voltage give it for common conditions.

It operates from 4.5 V to 36 V (±2.25 V to ±18 V); above 40 V (±20 V) total the device can be damaged. There is a single operating mode, active whenever the supply is above 4.5 V. Performance is specified at ±15 V with a mid-supply reference; it also works with non-mid-supply references, and the typical curves show what changes with supply and reference.

The output is developed with respect to REF. With dual supplies REF usually goes to a low-impedance ground; with a single supply it is driven to a level such as mid-supply (2.5 V on 5 V) to shift the output for an ADC. Any resistance in series with REF adds to one internal 10 kΩ resistor, unbalances the difference amplifier and lowers CMRR; keep it under 5 Ω. A voltage reference drives it well; a resistor divider needs an op amp buffer.

Input impedance is about 100 GΩ and bias current is typically 150 pA, changing little with input voltage. Both inputs need a DC path for that current; without one they drift outside the common-mode range and saturate the input amplifiers. A low-resistance source can return through one input to ground (thermocouple); a higher-impedance source does better with two equal resistors, one per input, which lowers bias-current offset and improves high-frequency CMRR; a transformer can return through its centre tap.

At G = 1 the gain error is lowest, because the difference amplifier's resistors track. Above G = 1, gain error and gain drift grow from the 24.7 kΩ feedback resistors working against RG, and except at very high gain the gain drift is the largest drift term. Input-stage errors dominate at high gain, while output-stage errors shrink by the gain when referred to the input. For a 1 V output the input signal is 1 mV at G = 1000; the error budget is worked at G = 1, 100 and 1000 with every term referred to the input. Static errors can be calibrated out in production; drift then limits the system.

Requirements: 4 mA to 20 mA and ±20 mA inputs with under 20 Ω burden and at most ±0.4 V burden voltage, a ±10 V input of about 100 kΩ, output within 0 V to 5 V. R1 = 100 kΩ sets the voltage-mode input impedance; a larger value adds noise. R3 = 20 Ω is small against R1 and R2 and gives ±400 mV at ±20 mA. R1 and R2 are 0.1 % parts.

Match the two input paths in source impedance and capacitance so common-mode signals are not turned into differential ones; even a small capacitance mismatch at the RG pins lowers CMRR over frequency, so gain-switching parts on RG (switches, PhotoMOS relays) should have low and matched capacitance. Bypass each supply pin to ground with a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor close to the device; one capacitor from V+ to ground serves a single supply. Keep input traces away from supply and output traces, and cross them at right angles where they must meet. Place external parts, especially RG, close to the pins, keep traces short, connect the exposed pad to -V, use ground pours to shield the input pair, and give REF a low-impedance connection.
